meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'how; as', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How was it in Hungary?
As you all know...
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'нимать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to understand', paired with 'понять'.

examples.trans: I understand.
I want to go to the sea, you know?

examples.text: Я хочу нормально жить! Я хочу биде, понимаешь?
examples.trans: I want to live like a normal person! I want a bidet, do you understand?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to take', paired with 'взять'.

examples.trans: I'm not taking the knife.
Chef, I didn't take it.
We have to take all the money.

meanings.note: Common Russian noun meaning 'money' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I have no money.
The money is on the table.
Gum? I didn't have enough money.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Grab him!
It needs a wash.
Four-eyes! Grab him!

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'сутствие'). Common neuter noun meaning 'presence' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: В его присутствии было некое мельфо.
examples.trans: In his presence was simply not proper.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новое присутствие.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new presence.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'a certain, some kind of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: В его присутствии было некое мельфо.
examples.trans: In his presence was simply not proper.

examples.text: Макс сразу сказал «некий» и вернулся к плите.
examples.trans: Max immediately said 'a certain' and returned to the stove.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'mille-feuille pastry' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: В его присутствии было некое мельфо.
examples.trans: In his presence was simply not proper.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новый мильфей.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new mille-feuille pastry.

meanings.note: Prefix 'во-' ('into, up') marks inward or upward movement (stem 'обще').

examples.trans: That's no problem at all.
I have no idea at all.

examples.text: Я человек чистый. Я вообще не вор.
examples.trans: I'm an honest man. I'm not a thief at all.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'лжен'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('must, should; owe').

examples.trans: I have to work.
Greed should be moderate.

examples.text: Жадность, Паша, должна быть умеренная. Комнатной температуры.
examples.trans: Greed, Pasha, should be moderate. Room temperature.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'about', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm thinking about it.
We're talking about the town.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'this', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This house.
I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'знать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to recognise; to find out', paired with 'узнавать'.

examples.trans: Did you recognise me?
I'll find out where he is.
You recognised me. Thanks for seeing me.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'now', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Теперь я начальник нашей стройки. Ты уволен!
examples.trans: Now I'm the boss of our building site. You're fired!

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.
Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'nothing', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: There's nothing left.
I don't know anything.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

получиться.gloss: to turn out, to work out

meanings.en: to turn out, to work out
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'лучиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to turn out, to work out', paired with 'получаться'.

examples.trans: It will all work out!
He'll make a good doctor.

examples.text: Классный из тебя мэр получится, Самсон.
examples.trans: You'll make a great mayor, Samson.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'over, above; at', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The lamp is above the table.
Don't laugh at me.

examples.text: За поведение? Вы смеётесь надо мной?
examples.trans: For my conduct? Are you laughing at me?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'go, walk', paired with 'пойти'.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

examples.text: Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: That's why I'm running for a second term.

examples.text: А ты иди на биржу труда. Там есть работа.
examples.trans: You go to the job centre. There's work there.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'знаваться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to confess'.

examples.trans: We have to go and confess honestly.
You have to know how to confess, let's go.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'читать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to read (through), to finish reading', paired with 'читать'.

examples.trans: I read Machiavelli, that book The Prince.
What else should I read here?

examples.text: Я прочитаю этот рецепт и приготовлю блюдо.
examples.trans: I will read this recipe and prepare the dish.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
Too much to do.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'detective story, detective' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Анастасия Степановна, я прочитал много детективов.
examples.trans: Anastasiya Stepanovna, I have read a great many detective novels.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новый детектив.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new detective story.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'верить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to believe', paired with 'верить'.

examples.trans: And everyone believed it?
Believe me.

examples.text: Со своего телефона? И все поверили?
examples.trans: From your own phone? And everyone believed it?

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'знание'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'confession, admission' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: He wrote a full confession.
That was an unexpected admission.

examples.text: Предлагаю чистосердечное признание. Дадут всего восемь лет.
examples.trans: I suggest a full confession. They'll give you only eight years.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, that; it is', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's mine.
And this is for you.
And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('extreme, end, last').

examples.text: Но, по крайней мере, он дочь свою любит!
examples.trans: But at least he loves his daughter!
Who is last in the queue?

examples.text: Витя, я выражаю тебе своё крайнее возмущение!
examples.trans: Vitya, I express to you my extreme outrage!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'option, variant, choice' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Пробуем, других вариантов у нас нет.
examples.trans: Let's try it, we have no other options.

examples.text: Это самый лучший вариант для всех.
examples.trans: This is the very best option for everyone.

examples.text: Трава, говорите? Отлично! Пробуем, других вариантов у нас нет.
examples.trans: Herbs, you say? Excellent! Let's try it, we have no other options.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I'm just tired.
It's easy.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

забрать.gloss: to take back, to take away

meanings.en: to take back, to take away
meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'брать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to take back, to take away', paired with 'забирать'.

examples.trans: He will withdraw the statement.
I'll take the keys.

examples.text: Поговори с Аракеляном. Пусть он заберёт заявление.
examples.trans: Talk to Arakelyan. Get him to withdraw his statement.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'without', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's no problem.
This time there's no trick.
That's no problem at all.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('personal, private').

examples.trans: That's a personal question.
I have my own driver.

examples.text: Всё, Нинок. Теперь у нас есть личный слуга.
examples.trans: That's it, Ninok. Now we have our own personal servant.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'contact' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: All contacts go only through me.
Do you have his contact details?

examples.text: Будут разные провокации. Все контакты только через меня.
examples.trans: There will be various provocations. All contacts go only through me.

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'брый'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('kind; good').

examples.trans: Good evening!
She is very kind.

examples.text: Добрый вечер, Вика. С Новым годом!
examples.trans: Good evening, Vika. Happy New Year!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'day' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Good afternoon!
I'll call in the next few days.
Any day now, on the website.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'would', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

examples.text: Юле бы дублёнку купили, Славику бы ноутбук.
examples.trans: We could have bought Yulia a sheepskin coat, and Slavik a laptop.
Look who's talking.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: I want coffee.
If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'пить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to have a drink'.

related.gloss: to to have a drink (base verb)
not to to have a drink (negated infinitive)

examples.text: Самсон, ты с ума сошёл? Ты так воды пошёл попить?
examples.trans: Samson, have you lost your mind? Is that how you went for a drink of water?

examples.text: Я пирожные принёс! Может, мы пока чаю попьём?
examples.trans: I brought pastries! Maybe we could have some tea in the meantime?

examples.text: Самсонов, успокойся! Аркаша был занят. И мы пригласили Даню чай попить.
examples.trans: Samsonov, calm down! Arkasha was busy. And we invited Danya to have some tea.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, by; (у меня) I have', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
He's at our place.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to order', paired with 'заказывать'.

examples.trans: Maybe we should order?
We ordered tea and sandwiches.

examples.text: Если опоздают, пицца бесплатно. Может, закажем?
examples.trans: If they're late, the pizza is free. Maybe we should order?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'колько'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: So much gum!
How much is it?
So much gum! Cool!
